```{r setup}
library(CDCAtlas)
library(dplyr)
```

## Overview

CDC AtlasPlus reports many outcomes at the county level. For some analyses,
especially geographic access analyses, we may want estimates at a smaller
geographic unit: the Census tract or block group.

`CDCAtlas` estimates these in three steps:

1. `impute_suppressed()` fills in county counts CDC suppressed.
2. `no_county_cases()` reports cases in each state's total that no county
   accounts for.
3. `extrapolate_from_county()` shares each county's count across its tracts
   (or, with `to = "block group"`, its block groups) using Census
   populations.

This article uses tracts throughout; block groups work the same way.

The basic idea is:

1. Retrieve county-level CDC AtlasPlus counts.
2. Retrieve tract-level Census population denominators.
3. Match each tract to its parent county.
4. Allocate each county's reported cases across tracts in proportion to the
   tract's share of the relevant county population.

For example, if a tract contains 2% of a county's population in the relevant
denominator, it receives 2% of the county's reported cases.

This is a **population-weighted extrapolation**, not a direct CDC tract-level
surveillance estimate.

## Census data requirements

Tract-level extrapolation requires tract-level population denominators from the
U.S. Census Bureau. `CDCAtlas` uses the `tidycensus` package to retrieve these
denominators.

If you only use `CDCAtlas` to retrieve AtlasPlus county, state, or national data,
you do not need to set up `tidycensus`. However, if you use
`extrapolate_from_county()`, you will need:

1. the `tidycensus` package installed
2. a Census API key
3. the API key saved in your R environment

You can install `tidycensus` (version 1.8.0 or later) from CRAN:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("tidycensus")
```

Then request a free Census API key from the U.S. Census Bureau and save it
with `tidycensus::census_api_key()`. With `install = TRUE` it is written to your
`.Renviron` file as `CENSUS_API_KEY`, so it is there in future sessions:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
tidycensus::census_api_key("YOUR KEY HERE", install = TRUE)
readRenviron("~/.Renviron") # or restart R
```

Without `install = TRUE`, the key lasts only for the current session.

See [https://walker-data.com/tidycensus/](https://walker-data.com/tidycensus/) for further details.

## Important assumptions

This method assumes that, within each county and stratum, cases are distributed
across tracts in proportion to the relevant Census denominator.

For example:

- unstratified HIV prevalence may be allocated using total tract population
- sex-stratified counts may be allocated using tract population by sex
- age-stratified counts may be allocated using tract population by age
- race/ethnicity-stratified counts may be allocated using tract population by
  race/ethnicity

This can be useful for geographic access models, but it should not be interpreted
as observed tract-level surveillance data.

## Basic unstratified extrapolation

The simplest use case is extrapolating county-level data to tracts using total
tract population.

```{r, message = TRUE, warning = TRUE}
hiv_tract <- get_atlas(
  disease = "hiv",
  year = 2022,
  geography = "county"
) |>
  impute_suppressed() |>
  extrapolate_from_county()
```

`impute_suppressed()` and `extrapolate_from_county()` report what they could
not estimate or allocate. Those messages are shown here on purpose: they say
which cases are missing from the tract estimates.

The returned data contain one row per tract and indicator (here, HIV
diagnoses and HIV prevalence), with the county-level AtlasPlus count
allocated to tracts.

```{r}
head(hiv_tract)
```

A typical output includes columns such as:

```{r}
names(hiv_tract)
```

The main columns are:

- `geoid` and `area_name`: the tract
- `county_fips` and `county_name`: the county it is in
- `indicator` and `year`: what was counted, and when; `acs_year` is the ACS
  year of the population figures
- `county_cases`: the county's count, and `county_cases_allocated`: the cases
  shared across the county's tracts
- `area_population_acs` and `county_population_acs`: the ACS population of
  the tract and of the county's tracts
- `area_cases`: the estimated cases in the tract

See `?extrapolate_from_county` for every column.

The key calculation is:

```r
area_cases = county_cases_allocated * area_population_acs / county_population_acs
```

With the default options, `county_cases_allocated` is the county's own count.
It also includes any cases with no county that `no_county = "spread"` adds, and
any cases of unknown race that `unknown_race = "redistribute"` adds.

## Checking county totals

After extrapolation, tract-level estimates should sum back to the county
counts they share out (`county_cases_allocated`), allowing for small
floating-point differences.

```{r, message = TRUE, warning = TRUE}
hiv_tract |>
  group_by(county_fips, indicator) |>
  summarize(
    county_cases = first(county_cases_allocated),
    tract_cases_sum = sum(area_cases, na.rm = TRUE),
    difference = tract_cases_sum - county_cases,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(difference))) |>
  head()
```

In a clean allocation, the `difference` column should be very close to zero.

## County rows that were not allocated

Some county rows can't be shared across tracts. They are listed, with a reason,
in an attribute of the result:

```{r}
attr(hiv_tract, "not_allocated") |>
  count(reason, indicator)
```

Reasons include counties CDC has no data for ("Data not available" with no
count), counties with no Census tracts in the ACS year, strata with no Census
population (race "Other", for example), and suppressed counties that
`impute_suppressed()` could not estimate. In CDC's 2022 data, for example,
Valdez-Cordova Census Area, Alaska, is still listed although it was split into
two census areas in 2019; it is suppressed, has no CDC population and has no
2022 tracts, so it is left out. Use `extrapolate_from_county(unestimated =
"error")` to stop instead.

Cases in state totals with no county are reported separately:

```{r}
attr(hiv_tract, "no_county_cases") |>
  head()
```

## Sex-stratified extrapolation

For sex-stratified AtlasPlus data, the allocation denominator should also be
sex-specific.

```{r, message = TRUE, warning = TRUE}
hiv_tract_sex <- get_atlas(
  disease = "hiv",
  year = 2022,
  geography = "county",
  stratify_by = "sex"
) |>
  impute_suppressed() |>
  extrapolate_from_county()
```

This means that male county cases are allocated across tracts using the male
population in each tract, and female county cases are allocated using the female
population in each tract.

Conceptually:

$$
\widehat{\text{tract cases}}_{\text{male}} =
\text{county cases}_{\text{male}} \times
\frac{\text{tract population}_{\text{male}}}
{\text{county population}_{\text{male}}}
$$

$$
\widehat{\text{tract cases}}_{\text{female}} =
\text{county cases}_{\text{female}} \times
\frac{\text{tract population}_{\text{female}}}
{\text{county population}_{\text{female}}}
$$
The resulting data should include one row per tract, indicator and sex.

```{r, message = TRUE, warning = TRUE}
hiv_tract_sex |>
  count(sex, indicator)
```

You can verify the allocation within each county and sex stratum.

```{r, message = TRUE, warning = TRUE}
hiv_tract_sex |>
  group_by(county_fips, sex, indicator) |>
  summarize(
    county_cases = first(county_cases_allocated),
    tract_cases_sum = sum(area_cases, na.rm = TRUE),
    difference = tract_cases_sum - county_cases,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(difference))) |>
  head()
```

## Age-stratified extrapolation

Age-stratified extrapolation works the same way, except that the Census
denominator is based on tract population within the corresponding AtlasPlus age
group.

```{r, message = TRUE, warning = TRUE}
hiv_tract_age <- get_atlas(
  disease = "hiv",
  year = 2022,
  geography = "county",
  stratify_by = "age"
) |>
  impute_suppressed() |>
  extrapolate_from_county()
```

The output contains one row per tract, indicator and age group.

```{r, message = TRUE, warning = TRUE}
hiv_tract_age |>
  count(age, indicator)
```

Again, the diagnostic check is whether tract estimates sum back to the original
county count within each county-age stratum.

```{r, message = TRUE, warning = TRUE}
hiv_tract_age |>
  group_by(county_fips, age, indicator) |>
  summarize(
    county_cases = first(county_cases_allocated),
    tract_cases_sum = sum(area_cases, na.rm = TRUE),
    difference = tract_cases_sum - county_cases,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(difference))) |>
  head()
```

## Race/ethnicity-stratified extrapolation

CDC AtlasPlus commonly uses a combined race/ethnicity variable. For example,
Hispanic/Latino is represented as a single ethnicity category, while the
remaining groups are usually non-Hispanic race categories.

```{r, message = TRUE, warning = TRUE}
hiv_tract_race <- get_atlas(
  disease = "hiv",
  year = 2022,
  geography = "county",
  stratify_by = "race"
) |>
  impute_suppressed() |>
  extrapolate_from_county()
```

The tract populations come from ACS table B03002 (Hispanic or Latino origin
by race), whose groups match AtlasPlus's: Hispanic/Latino of any race, and
non-Hispanic groups for the others. B03002 has no ages, so for HIV each
tract's race populations are scaled by its share of residents aged 13 and
older. `race_table = "B01001"` uses the race-specific sex-by-age tables
instead, which have ages but match AtlasPlus's groups only for White and
Hispanic. "Other" and "Unknown" have no Census population, so they are left
out (see the next section for "Unknown").

```{r, message = TRUE, warning = TRUE}
hiv_tract_race |>
  count(race_ethnicity, indicator)
```

## Choices you can change

Each default can be changed in `extrapolate_from_county()`; see
`?extrapolate_from_county` for the details.

| Situation | Default | Alternative |
|---|---|---|
| Cases in a state's total that no county accounts for | Left out and reported (`no_county = "report"`) | `no_county = "spread"` shares them across the state's counties, by population or by cases (`spread_by`). Not available for CDC's HIV estimates, whose county data cover only Ending the HIV Epidemic counties. |
| A county has cases in a stratum but no Census population in any of its tracts | Shared by the tracts' total population (`empty_strata = "total"`) | `"equal"` shares equally across tracts; `"none"` keeps the tract rows with `area_cases` as `NA`, with a warning. |
| Cases of unknown race or age | Left out and listed (`unknown_race`, `unknown_age = "report"`) | `"redistribute"` shares them across the county's known groups in proportion to their counts. |
| Suppressed counties `impute_suppressed()` couldn't estimate | Left out and listed (`unestimated = "leave out"`) | `"error"` stops. |
| A tract with no ACS population figure | The whole county stratum (that county, indicator, year and group) is left out and listed, so cases aren't shared over an incomplete denominator (`missing_population = "leave out"`) | `"error"` stops. |
| Which ACS release | The 5-year release ending in the data year | `acs_year` sets it. |

County rows left out are listed, with the reason, in
`attr(result, "not_allocated")`. With `empty_strata = "none"`, the tract rows
stay in the result with `area_cases` as `NA` instead.

## Older years and Census geography

CDC reports every year on its current county map, while each ACS release uses
the tract map of its own years. The package assigns 2010 tracts in
Connecticut and Alaska to CDC's current counties, so ACS releases from 2010 to
2019 cover them. A few combinations aren't covered, such as Connecticut with
the 2020 and 2021 releases; those counties are left out with a warning that
says why. [About CDC AtlasPlus data](about-atlasplus-data.html#cdcs-county-map)
lists them.

### The one tract in two counties

One 2010 tract in Connecticut (GEOID 09013890201) lies in two of CDC's current
counties, the Capitol and Northeastern Connecticut planning regions. With ACS
releases from 2010 to 2019, the result has two rows for it, one in each
planning region, and two rows for each of its block groups with
`to = "block group"`. So `geoid` is unique within `county_fips`, not overall,
and `extrapolate_from_county()` warns when this happens.

Each row holds a share of the tract: its ACS populations are multiplied by the
share of the tract's land area in that planning region (about 39% and 61%),
and its cases are that planning region's count shared over them. A block group
gets its parent tract's shares, which are not measured shares of the block
group's own population.

Before joining to boundaries, which have each tract once, sum the area columns
by `geoid` within year, indicator and stratum:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
hiv_tract_2017 <- get_atlas(
  disease = "hiv",
  year = 2017,
  geography = "county"
) |>
  impute_suppressed() |>
  extrapolate_from_county()

hiv_tract_2017_one_row <- hiv_tract_2017 |>
  summarize(
    area_cases = sum(area_cases),
    area_population_acs = sum(area_population_acs),
    area_total_population = sum(area_total_population),
    .by = c(year, indicator, race_ethnicity, sex, age, geoid, area_name)
  )
```

Sum all three columns: keeping only one of the two rows, or the first
population, would understate the tract. The county columns (`county_fips`,
`county_cases`, `county_population_acs` and the rest) are left out of the
summary because the combined row belongs to two counties; they repeat on
every tract of a county, so they should not be summed across tracts either.

## Multiple stratification variables

`extrapolate_from_county()` takes data stratified by at most one variable.
`get_atlas()` can download two-way strata (sex by age, for example), but these
can't be extrapolated yet.

## Working with geometry

The results have Census GEOIDs (`geoid`) but no boundaries. To map them, join
them to tract boundaries, for example from the tigris package. With ACS
releases from 2010 to 2019, first sum the one tract that is in two counties
(see [The one tract in two counties](#the-one-tract-in-two-counties)).
